title: Promote The Partner Who Already Runs Half The Company
excerptForBlog:
Ted Sarandos appointed co-CEO and elected to Board of Directors. Ted joined Netflix over 20 years ago, and we are thrilled to appoint him to be co-CEO with Reed. "Ted has been my partner for decades. This change makes formal what was already informal -- that Ted and I share the leadership of Netflix," says Hastings. Lead Independent director Jay Hoag says "Having watched Reed and Ted work together for so long, the board and I are confident this is the right step to evolve Netflix's management structure so that we can continue to best serve our members and shareholders for years to come." Ted will also continue to serve as Chief Content Officer. In addition, Greg Peters has been appointed COO adding to his Chief Product Officer role. "We want Greg to help us stay aligned and effective as we grow so quickly around the world," said Hastings.

In Q2, revenue grew 25% year over year, while quarterly operating income exceeded $1 billion. We added a Q2-record 10.1m paid memberships vs. 2.7m in last year's Q2. In the first half of this year, we've added 26m paid memberships, nearly on par with the 28m we achieved in all of 2019. However, growth is slowing as consumers get through the initial shock of Covid and social restrictions. We forecast 2.5m paid net adds for Q3'20 vs. 6.8m in the prior year quarter.

lessonTitle: Promote The Partner Who Already Runs Half The Company
pullQuote: Formalizing power someone already has is cheaper than losing them — and clearer for everyone watching.
leadershipTraits: formalizes reality instead of hiding it
times hard announcements with strong results
situation: On July 16, 2020, Netflix filed its Q2 shareholder letter with the SEC. The headline news was not the record 10.1 million paid memberships added in the quarter. It was a structural announcement: Ted Sarandos, already Chief Content Officer for over 20 years, was named co-CEO and joined the board. Greg Peters, already Chief Product Officer, was simultaneously named COO.
insight:
Reed Hastings' own words reveal the logic plainly: 'This change makes formal what was already informal — that Ted and I share the leadership of Netflix.' That is not a modest aside. It is a precise description of a real organizational principle — if two people already share power in practice, the org chart should say so. Leaving informal power informal creates fragility: the arrangement depends entirely on the relationship holding. Making it formal makes it durable, succession-ready, and visible to the board, investors, and the organization itself.

The Peters move follows the same logic. As Netflix was adding 26 million paid members in six months — nearly matching all of 2019 — Hastings wrote that he wanted Peters 'to help us stay aligned and effective as we grow so quickly around the world.' Fast growth strains coordination. Adding an operational layer (COO) to an existing product leader is a classic **span-of-control** response: when growth outpaces your structure, you add coordination capacity before the cracks appear, not after.
application: Audit your own informal power structure. Who already makes the calls, holds the relationships, or carries the institutional knowledge that keeps things running? If a key person left tomorrow and their role wasn't in the org chart, that's a gap. Name the real structure before a crisis forces you to.
